chapters.name: Chapter 1: Designing a team of agents

lessons.title: Lesson 1: When one agent is enough, and when it is not
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Decide whether a task needs more than one agent.
This lesson builds toward: Given a job you might automate, you will decide whether it needs one agent or a team, using the hiring test, with a one-sentence reason for each job.
Start with one agent. Every extra agent adds model calls (cost and time), handoffs (places to lose information) and more things to test. Many tasks that look like they need a team work fine with one well-prompted agent and good tools.
Consider more than one agent when: the job has clearly different skills (research, then writing, then checking); one prompt is getting too long and confused; you want an independent check, since a reviewer with fresh instructions catches mistakes the writer misses; or parts can run at the same time.
A useful test: if you would hire two different people for it, two agents may help. If one person could do it with a checklist, one agent with a checklist is probably better.
Words to know:
- Multi-agent system: several AI agents, each with its own role, working together on one job.
- Handoff: passing work and information from one agent to another.
- Overhead: the extra cost and effort a design adds.
Try it now: List three jobs you might automate. For each, write "one agent" or "team" and one sentence on why, using the hiring test.
You can now decide when a task truly needs more than one agent.

options: Asking whether a person would pass a job interview
Testing whether a model can be hired by a company
Asking whether you would hire two different people for this job
Counting how many tools a job needs
check.why: If you would not hire two people, one agent is usually enough.

check.q: A job is sorting messages into four categories with a checklist. What would you build?
options: One agent with clear instructions
A team of four agents, one per category
An orchestrator with workers
A writer and a reviewer
check.why: A simple, well-defined job does not need the extra cost and handoffs of a team.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Common patterns: pipeline, orchestrator, reviewer
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Pick a multi-agent pattern that fits a task.
This lesson builds toward: Given a job that needs a team, you will choose a pattern (pipeline, orchestrator and workers, or writer and reviewer) and draw how work passes between agents, labeling what passes along each arrow.
Pipeline: agents work in a fixed order, each passing its output to the next, like an assembly line: research, then write, then format. Simple to build and to debug, because you always know who acts next.
Orchestrator and workers: one agent (the orchestrator) breaks the goal into parts, hands each part to a worker agent, then combines the results. Flexible, but the orchestrator can split the work badly, and more freedom means more to check.
Writer and reviewer: one agent produces, a second judges against a checklist and either approves or sends it back with reasons. This is the most useful pattern for beginners because it adds an independent quality check. It needs a round limit so the two never argue forever.
Words to know:
- Pipeline: agents working in a fixed order, each passing work to the next.
- Orchestrator: an agent that splits a goal into tasks and hands them to other agents.
- Reviewer agent: an agent that checks another agent's work against clear rules.
Try it now: For the "team" job from Lesson 1, draw the agents as boxes with arrows (on paper is fine). Label which pattern it is and what passes along each arrow.
You can now choose between a pipeline, an orchestrator with workers, and a writer with a reviewer.

check.q: What does the orchestrator do in an orchestrator-and-workers pattern?
options: Checks every draft against a checklist
Splits the goal and hands parts to workers
Saves files to disk
Runs only at the end
check.why: The orchestrator divides the work and passes parts to worker agents.

check.q: Your job always goes research, then write, then format, in that order. Which pattern fits?
options: Writer and reviewer
Orchestrator and workers
No pattern; use three chatbots
Pipeline
check.why: A fixed order of steps is a pipeline, which is also easy to debug.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Writing roles and handoffs
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Write a role prompt for each agent and a handoff format between them.
This lesson builds toward: For each agent in the team, you will write a role prompt and a JSON handoff format, with one job per agent and a reviewer checklist that can be checked.
Each agent gets its own short system prompt: who it is, its one job, its tools (only what it needs), and its output format. The writer does not need the reviewer's checklist in full; the reviewer does not need writing tools at all.
The handoff is the message passed between agents. Make it structured, not chatty: {"draft": "...", "facts_used": [...]} from writer to reviewer, and {"decision": "approve" or "revise", "reasons": [...]} back. Structured handoffs make it obvious what was passed and easy for code to check.
Give the reviewer a checklist, not a feeling. "Is it good?" gets agreement. "Does every fact appear in the fact sheet? Is it under 80 words? Does it avoid the words best and guaranteed?" gets a real check.
Step by step:
- Write a role prompt for each agent: role, one job, tools, output format.
- Give each agent only the tools it needs.
- Define the handoff as JSON with fixed keys.
- Write the reviewer's checklist as yes/no questions.
Words to know:
- Role prompt: the system prompt that gives one agent its job and rules.
- Checklist: a list of specific yes/no checks used to judge work.
Try it now: Write the writer's role prompt, the reviewer's role prompt with a 3-item checklist, and the two JSON handoff formats for the final-task system.
You can now write role prompts and structured handoffs for a team of agents.

check.q: What belongs in a role prompt?
options: The agent's one job, its tools and its output format
Every other agent's instructions
Your API key
A list of all past runs
check.why: A role prompt keeps each agent focused on its own job and format.

check.q: Your reviewer is told "Check if the draft is good." What would you change?
options: Nothing, it is short
Give it writing tools so it can fix drafts
Replace it with a checklist of specific questions it can answer yes or no
Let it decide its own rules
check.why: Vague review questions lead to agreeing too easily; a checklist gives a real check.

chapters.name: Chapter 2: Building and testing the team

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Shared state: one place for the work
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Keep a team's work in one shared state that every agent reads from.
This lesson builds toward: In your Python code, you will keep the team's work in one shared state that only your code updates, logging the state after each step.
Shared state is one place where the team's work lives, owned by your code, not by any agent. In Python, a dictionary works: state = {'facts': FACTS, 'draft': None, 'reviews': [], 'round': 0, 'status': 'drafting'}.
Each agent gets only the parts it needs and returns a handoff; your code checks the handoff and updates state. The writer reads facts and the last review; the reviewer reads facts and the draft. No agent edits state directly.
This keeps the truth in one place, makes the log easy (save state after each step), and stops agents from passing around copies that drift apart. If one agent's output is bad, your code can refuse it before it reaches the next agent.
Step by step:
- Create a state dictionary with every field the team needs.
- Give each agent only the fields it needs.
- Check each handoff in code before updating state.
- Save a copy of state to the log after each step.
Words to know:
- Shared state: the single record of a team's work that the code keeps and every agent reads from.
- Drift: when copies of information slowly become different from each other.
Try it now: Create the state dictionary for the final task. Write two functions, run_writer(state) and run_reviewer(state), that each call ask_model with their role prompt and return parsed JSON, without changing state themselves.
You can now keep a multi-agent system's work in one shared state controlled by your code.

check.q: What is shared state in a multi-agent system?
options: Each agent's private notes
One place, owned by your code, that holds the team's work
The model's memory between days
A shared password
check.why: One shared state that your code updates keeps every agent working from the same facts.

check.q: The writer and reviewer each keep their own copy of the draft, and the copies start to differ. What would you do?
options: Let each agent update the state directly
Add a third agent to merge them
Ignore it if the final answer looks fine
Keep one shared state that only your code updates after checking each handoff
check.why: Separate copies drift; one checked shared state prevents it.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Stopping loops and keeping humans in charge
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Add a round limit and a human escalation to a writer-reviewer loop.
This lesson builds toward: Given a writer-reviewer loop, you will add a round limit and hand unresolved work to a person, stopping with needs_human after at most 3 rounds.
Two agents can loop forever: the reviewer always finds something, the writer always changes something. Set MAX_ROUNDS = 3. If the reviewer has not approved by then, stop with status 'needs_human' and show the last draft and the reasons.
Watch for two other team failures. Rubber-stamping: the reviewer approves everything, often because its checklist is vague. Ping-pong: the writer fixes one problem and brings back an old one. Read the log for both.
Keep humans in charge of the result. The team produces a draft and a review; a person approves anything that will be published, sent or used to make a decision. More agents do not remove the need for that checkpoint; they make it more important.
Step by step:
- Set MAX_ROUNDS.
- Loop: writer drafts, reviewer decides.
- On approve: status 'approved', stop.
- On revise: pass the reasons back to the writer.
- At the limit: status 'needs_human', show the draft and reasons.
Words to know:
- Round: one cycle of draft and review.
- Rubber-stamping: approving everything without really checking.
- Escalation: handing a problem to a person when the system cannot settle it.
Try it now: Write the writer-reviewer loop with MAX_ROUNDS = 3. Test it with a fact sheet where the writer is likely to exaggerate. Then test the limit by making the reviewer's checklist impossible ("under 5 words") and confirm it stops with needs_human.
You can now stop agent ping-pong with a round limit and hand unresolved work to a person.

check.q: What is ping-pong in a writer-reviewer loop?
options: Fixing one problem brings back an old one, round after round
The reviewer approving every draft
Two agents running at the same time
A fast loop that finishes in one round
check.why: Ping-pong is endless back-and-forth, which is why the loop needs a round limit.

check.q: The reviewer has not approved after 3 rounds. What should the system do?
options: Approve the last draft anyway
Start again with round 1
Stop with needs_human and show the draft and the reasons
Raise the limit to 10 rounds
check.why: Unresolved work goes to a person with everything they need to decide.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Does the team beat one agent? Testing it
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Compare a multi-agent system with a single agent on the same tests.
This lesson builds toward: Given the same test inputs, you will compare the team with a single-agent baseline on quality and model calls, scoring both with the same checklist and choosing the simpler one when scores tie.
A team is only worth it if it does better. Test it the way you tested prompts in course 2: the same inputs, a clear score, and a comparison. Make three fact sheets, run them through the team and through a single agent that has the checklist in its own prompt.
Score each output with the reviewer's checklist yourself (not with the reviewer agent), and count model calls for each approach. Model calls stand in for cost and time.
Write the result honestly. If the single agent scored the same with a third of the calls, use the single agent. If the team caught real mistakes the single agent missed, the extra calls bought you quality. Either answer is a good engineering result.
Step by step:
- Make three test fact sheets.
- Run each through the team and through a single agent.
- Score every output yourself with the checklist.
- Count model calls for each approach.
- Write which approach wins and why.
Words to know:
- Baseline: the simple version you compare against, here a single agent.
- Model call: one request to the model; more calls mean more cost and time.
Try it now: Final task: finish the writer-reviewer system with shared state, structured handoffs and MAX_ROUNDS = 3, run it on three fact sheets, run a single-agent baseline on the same sheets, and write a short comparison of quality and model calls.
You can now build a small multi-agent system and prove whether it beats a single agent.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Clear roles and checklist Roles overlap, or the reviewer only asks whether the draft is good. The writer and reviewer each have one job; the reviewer checks facts from the sheet, under 80 words and no claims like "best". The reviewer has no writing tools and gives a reason for every revise. Structured handoffs Agents pass free text the code cannot check. The reviewer returns JSON with approve or revise and reasons. The code checks each handoff before using it. Shared state Agents keep separate copies of the work. The work passes through one state dictionary that the code updates. The state is logged after every step. Round limit and escalation No round limit, or the loop can run forever. Stops after at most 3 rounds and prints the full log. Unresolved work stops with needs_human and shows the draft and reasons. Fair comparison No single-agent baseline, or different inputs were used. The same 3 fact sheets were run through both, with a written note on which did better and why. Both were scored with the same checklist and model calls were counted. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: What is a baseline in this course?
options: The first draft the writer makes
A single agent you compare the team against
The lowest score allowed
The round limit
check.why: Comparing with a single agent shows whether the team is worth its extra cost.

check.q: The team scores a little higher than one agent but uses three times the model calls. What would you do?
options: Always pick the team, because teams are better
Stop testing
Add more agents to raise the score
Weigh whether the small gain is worth the extra cost and time, and write down why
check.why: Model calls stand for cost and time, so the choice weighs quality against them.
